# Passenger-Rail Corridor Proposal: Syracuse, NY to Rochester, NY

> **Illustrative estimates: costs, schedules and funding figures in this draft come from an uncalibrated planning model and approximate program parameters. They are not budgets or engineering estimates.**

## Executive Summary

This proposal evaluates three alignment options for intercity passenger rail service along the Syracuse, NY to Rochester, NY corridor. Based on 5000 simulation runs per alternative, Alternative 1 (the Existing corridor upgrade) achieves the highest composite score of 93.8 out of 100. It also offers the lowest median (P50) cost, the shortest median (P50) delivery schedule, and the shortest length among all options considered.

Alternative 1 utilizes an existing rail right-of-way for 99.2% of its route to serve Rochester and Syracuse, reaching a population of 1.25 million within a 10 miles buffer. Alternative 2 (the New direct alignment) trades existing right-of-way reuse for a greenfield path, while Alternative 3 (the Maximum population served) bends toward population centers to serve 1.28 million residents. State planning staff can leverage high-fitting federal grant programs to establish a comprehensive capital buildout strategy.

## Corridor Description

The Syracuse, NY to Rochester, NY passenger-rail corridor spans 77 miles to 82 miles depending on the alignment. All three alternatives connect 2 stations: Rochester and Syracuse. Population served within a 10 miles buffer ranges from 1.17 million to 1.28 million residents based on 2020 Census data.

Alternative 1 (Existing corridor upgrade) covers 77 miles with 99.2% of the line situated on existing rail, capturing 1.25 million residents with 8 environmental flag entries and 1 river crossings. Alternative 2 (New direct alignment) is 77 miles long with a 28.3% share on existing rail, serving 1.17 million residents with 3 environmental flag entries and 1 river crossings. Alternative 3 (Maximum population served) extends to 82 miles with a 73.0% share on existing rail, reaching 1.28 million residents with 4 environmental flag entries and 2 river crossings.

## Cost and Schedule Range

Costs discussed below represent illustrative estimates rather than final budgets, derived from per-mile benchmark placeholders. Risk profiles for capital costs and duration were generated using 5000 Monte Carlo simulation runs for each route option.

Alternative 1 features an estimated capital cost with a P10 of $1.6B, a median (P50) of $2.0B, and a P90 of $2.4B, alongside a time to opening with a P10 of 8.7 years, a median (P50) of 10.0 years, and a P90 of 11.4 years. Alternative 2 requires an estimated capital cost with a P10 of $3.2B, a median (P50) of $3.8B, and a P90 of $4.5B, with an estimated delivery schedule reflecting a P10 of 10.6 years, a median (P50) of 12.0 years, and a P90 of 13.5 years. Alternative 3 projects an estimated capital cost with a P10 of $2.5B, a median (P50) of $3.1B, and a P90 of $3.7B, with a schedule estimated at a P10 of 9.3 years, a median (P50) of 10.5 years, and a P90 of 11.9 years.

## Funding Strategy

The primary federal funding strategy targets the FRA Corridor Identification and Development Program (Corridor ID) as the initial planning entry point. For all options, Corridor ID offers a fit score of 0.95 and an estimated federal amount of $500K to support Step 1 scoping and pipeline placement. Capital funding for Alternative 1 targets the FRA Federal-State Partnership for Intercity Passenger Rail (National) program (fit score 0.90), which provides a federal amount of $1.6B, representing an 80.0% federal share of median cost.

Additional grant support for Alternative 1 includes FRA Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements (CRISI) with a fit score of 0.80, a federal amount of $250M, and a 12.8% federal share of median cost, as well as USDOT BUILD (formerly RAISE) Grants with a fit score of 0.45, a federal amount of $25M, and a 1.3% federal share of median cost. To cover the remaining non-federal match, USDOT Build America Bureau RRIF loans provide a fit score of 0.70 with a loan amount of $391M for Alternative 1, $758M for Alternative 2, and $615M for Alternative 3. For Alternative 2, the Federal-State Partnership grant provides $3.0B (79.1% federal share of median cost) but would require multi-phase awards because the median (P50) cost of $3.8B exceeds typical grant limits.

## Risks

Key project risks and environmental factors across the alternatives include:

* Environmental and Waterway Intersections: Alternative 1 contains 8 environmental flag entries and 1 river crossings. Alternative 2 involves 3 environmental flag entries and 1 river crossings, while Alternative 3 involves 4 environmental flag entries and 2 river crossings.
* Greenfield Acquisition and Alignment Complexity: Alternative 2 relies on only 28.3% existing rail right-of-way, significantly increasing land acquisition requirements compared to Alternative 1 (99.2%) and Alternative 3 (73.0%).
* Cost and Schedule Overruns: Capital cost estimates carry wide variance across P10 and P90 intervals (e.g., spanning from $3.2B to $4.5B for Alternative 2), while schedule uncertainties stretch delivery up to a P90 of 13.5 years.

## Next Steps

Recommended immediate actions for state DOT planners include:

* Submit an application to the FRA Corridor Identification and Development Program to secure $500K in planning funds and enter the federal project development pipeline.
* Initiate preliminary engineering studies and environmental reviews focusing on the 8 environmental flag entries and 1 river crossings identified along the preferred Alternative 1 alignment.
* Finalize non-federal funding match strategies, evaluating RRIF loan capacity alongside state legislative appropriations to cover required non-federal capital shares.
